title: Wine
wiki_lead:
Wine is an alcoholic drink made from fermented grape juice. It is produced and consumed in many regions around the world, in a wide variety of styles which are influenced by different varieties of grapes, growing environments, viticulture methods, and production techniques.
Wine has been produced for thousands of years, the earliest evidence dating from c. 6000 BCE in present-day Georgia. Its popularity spread around the Mediterranean during Classical antiquity, and was sustained in Western Europe by winemaking monks and a secular trade for general drinking. New World wine was established by settler colonies from the 16th century onwards, and the wine trade increased dramatically up to the latter half of the 19th century, when European vineyards were largely destroyed by the invasive pest phylloxera. After the Second World War, winemakers focused on quality and marketing to cater for a more discerning audience, and wine remains a popular drink in much of the world.
Wine has played an important role in religion since antiquity, and has featured prominently in the arts for centuries. It is drunk on its own and paired with food, often in social settings such as wine bars and restaurants. It is often tasted and assessed, with drinkers using a wide range of descriptors to communicate a wine's characteristics. Wine is also collected and stored, as an investment or to improve with age. Its alcohol content makes wine generally unhealthy to consume, although it may have cardioprotective benefits.

History

The earliest known traces of wine were found near Tbilisi, Georgia (c. 6000 BCE). The earliest known winery, from c. 4100 BCE, is the Areni-1 winery in Armenia. The subsequent spread of wine culture around the Mediterranean was probably due to the influence of the Phoenicians (from c. 1000 BCE) and Greeks (from c. 600 BCE). The Phoenicians exported the wines of Byblos, which were known for their quality into Roman times. Industrialized production of wine in ancient Greece spread across the Italian peninsula and to southern Gaul. The ancient Romans further increased the scale of wine production and trade networks, especially in Gaul around the time of the Gallic Wars.
In medieval Europe, monks grew grapes and made wine for the Eucharist. Monasteries expanded their land holdings over time and established vineyards in many of today's most successful wine regions. Bordeaux was a notable exception, being a purely commercial enterprise serving the Duchy of Aquitaine and by association Britain between the 12th and 15th centuries.

European wine grape traditions were incorporated into New World wine, with colonists planting vineyards in order to celebrate the Eucharist. Vineyards were established in Mexico by 1530, Peru by the 1550s and Chile shortly afterwards. The European settlement of South Africa and subsequent trade involving the Dutch East India Company led to the planting of vines in 1655. Jesuit Missionaries managed to grow vines in California in the 1670s, and plantings were later established in Los Angeles in the 1820s and Napa and Sonoma in the 1850s. Arthur Phillip introduced vines to Australia in 1788, and viticulture was widely practiced by the 1850s. The Australian missionary Samuel Marsden introduced vines to New Zealand in 1819.
The Great French Wine Blight began in the latter half of the 19th century, caused by an infestation of the aphid phylloxera brought over from America, whose louse stage feeds on vine roots and eventually kills the plant. Almost every vine in Europe needed to be replaced, by necessity grafted onto American rootstock which is naturally resistant to the pest. This practice continues to this day, with the exception of a small number of phylloxera-free wine regions such as South Australia.

grok_lead: Wine is the beverage resulting exclusively from the partial or complete alcoholic fermentation of fresh grapes, whether crushed or not, or of grape must. This process transforms the natural sugars in grape juice into alcohol and carbon dioxide, typically resulting in an alcoholic content between 8% and 15% by volume, though variations exist depending on style and region. The origins of wine production trace back to the Neolithic period, with archaeological evidence indicating grape domestication in the Transcaucasian regionâencompassing modern-day Georgia, Armenia, and Azerbaijanâbetween approximately 8500 and 4000 BCE. The earliest confirmed winemaking sites, dating to around 6000 BCE, have been uncovered in Georgia, where residues of tartaric acid (a grape-derived compound) were found in ancient pottery jars, suggesting intentional fermentation practices. From these ancient beginnings in the Near East and Caucasus, viticulture and winemaking spread through trade and migration to Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece, and Rome by the Bronze Age, evolving into a cornerstone of cultural, religious, and economic life across civilizations. Today, wine holds significant global cultural value, featured in rituals, cuisine, and social traditions, while also supporting a multibillion-dollar industry that influences agriculture, tourism, and international trade. Winemaking, or vinification, encompasses several key stages beginning with viticulture âthe cultivation of grapevines primarily from the species Vitis vinifera, which accounts for over 99% of global wine production. Grapes are harvested at optimal ripeness, typically by hand or machine, based on sugar levels, acidity, and phenolic maturity, often in late summer or autumn depending on climate and variety. Following harvest, the grapes undergo destemming and crushing to release juice (must), which is then fermented using natural or added yeast to convert sugars into alcohol over 7â14 days at controlled temperatures. Post-fermentation, processes like pressing (for white wines), malolactic fermentation (to soften acidity), clarification (to remove sediments), and aging in barrels or tanks develop flavor complexity, with the final product stabilized and bottled. These steps vary by wine style but emphasize minimal intervention to preserve terroir âthe unique environmental influences of soil, climate, and topography on grape character. Wines are broadly classified into still and sparkling varieties, with further distinctions by color, sweetness, and fortification. Still wines, the most common type, include red wines made from black-skinned grapes with skin contact during fermentation for color and tannins; white wines from white or black grapes pressed before fermentation, yielding lighter, crisp profiles; and rosÃ© wines produced via brief skin contact with black grapes or blending methods. Sparkling wines, such as Champagne or Prosecco, undergo a secondary fermentation to produce carbonation, often via the traditional method (bottle-fermented) or tank method (Charmat). Fortified wines, like Port or Sherry, have their alcohol content boosted to 15â22% by adding spirits during or after fermentation, while dessert wines (e.g., Sauternes) derive sweetness from botrytized grapes or late-harvest techniques. Sweetness levelsâdry (under 4g/L residual sugar), off-dry, semi-sweet, or sweetâare regulated internationally, with dry wines dominating global production. Global wine production centers on the Northern Hemisphere's Mediterranean climates, with the European Union accounting for about 45% of the world's 7.1 million hectares of vineyards. In 2024, total production reached 225.8 million hectolitres (mhl), the lowest since 1961, led by Italy (44.1 mhl), France (36.1 mhl), and Spain (31.0 mhl), followed by the United States (21.1 mhl) and Australia (10.2 mhl). Preliminary estimates for 2025 indicate a recovery to about 232 mhl, driven by improved weather in major regions like Italy and the United States. Consumption totaled 214.2 mhl, with the United States (33.3 mhl), France (23.0 mhl), and Italy (22.3 mhl) as top markets, reflecting a trend of declining volumes due to climate challenges, economic pressures, and shifting consumer preferences toward low- or no-alcohol alternatives. Key regions include Bordeaux and Tuscany for premium reds, Rioja and Napa Valley for bold varietals, and Marlborough ( New Zealand) for aromatic whites, all protected by geographical indications to ensure authenticity and quality.
